source.title: Sparse Attention Decomposition Applied to Circuit Tracing

record.tranche_reason: The study traces and intervenes on attention-head communication for GPT-2 small IOI, but uses sparse singular-vector decomposition rather than the original circuit-finding and evaluation recipe.
record.gate_note: The study tests IOI in GPT-2 small and reports trace structure and intervention effects. It cites prior circuit results for comparison, but those cited results are not recorded as findings of this study. The analysis is limited to heads firing on a token pair with more than 50% attention, and excludes MLP contributions and cases attending to the first token.
record.test_reason: The study traces IOI communication paths in GPT-2 small with a different circuit-finding method (sparse SVD 'singular vector tracing'). It compares the recovered heads with the original circuit and validates edges by ablating and boosting them, measured by the IO–S logit difference. Its overlap with the original circuit bears on V1 and V4. Its local-versus-global intervention differences bear on V5.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that attention scores are sparsely decomposable in the QK singular-vector basis. They find that tracing in this basis recovers a large part of the known IOI circuit plus new heads and redundant paths, and that the traced signals generally have causal effects on IOI performance. They acknowledge they do not build minimal circuits or explore all alternative paths.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SVD-based sparse attention decomposition and single-forward-pass tracing, followed by signal interventions. The original study used a different circuit-finding and evaluation recipe; this paper does not reproduce the original circuit criteria.
record.method_sensitivity: The effect on IO performance varies between global and local interventions and by target head; the local (9, 6) result reverses the general ablation pattern. The authors also report differences between parallel and serial multi-edge interventions.

fits_no_version.finding: Parallel-path ablations are frequently additive, while serial-path ablations are not. A lattice of redundant paths links layers 7–9, involving the three name movers and three S-inhibition heads.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The IOI circuit contains structured redundant parallel paths among S-inhibition and name-mover heads.

record.problems: The method only traces firing attention heads, ignores MLP contributions and first-token attention, and does not construct minimal circuits. The authors say the noise-separation rule may be too permissive and that the method does not explore all alternative pathways. Many intervention values are presented in figures without numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional outcome rows omitted. Several individual-edge intervention values appear only in plots and are not transcribed as separate rows because the text gives no numerical values for those individual edges.

untested.parts: The 26-head, 7-class circuit and the faithfulness, completeness and minimality criteria. The authors state they do not construct minimal circuits. MLPs and first-token attention are excluded.
Name movers are not ablated to measure backup-head compensation. The redundancy (backup name movers) is only inferred from local versus global differences.
Only GPT-2 small is studied; no other models, sizes, checkpoints or tasks.
No comparison of prompt distributions or of alternative metrics for circuit faithfulness. Ablation-type dependence is shown only for edge-level interventions.
There are no per-template or per-name-order results, and no prompts with more than two names.

missing.what: Ablating all outgoing edges of (2,8), a head not in the original circuit that attends to the verb, has a causal effect on the logit difference. This bears on V1 completeness and V4.
A trace that uses residuals directly instead of singular vectors misses most of the original circuit's heads. Recovery of the circuit depends on the tracing method.
Random-subspace ablation and boosting controls, shown in figures, generally have smaller effects than signal-subspace interventions.

record.verdict_notes: The record wrongly marked V4 untested: the study is itself an alternative circuit-finding method compared against the original circuit. V5 verdicts were changed from limits_scope to supports, because intervention-type dependence is what V5 asserts. Most intervention values appear only in figures. The (9,6) local reversal is described in the appendix text.

versions.untested_parts: Does not reproduce the 26-head, 7-class circuit or assess it using the original faithfulness, completeness, and minimality criteria. The authors explicitly say they do not construct minimal circuits.
Does not ablate the main name-mover heads to test whether backup heads take over their role.
Only GPT-2 small is studied; no other models, sizes, checkpoints, or other tasks are tested.
Does not compare circuit-finding methods for recovery of the same circuit. Random-subspace interventions are intervention controls, not alternative circuit-finding methods.
Does not compare prompt distributions or a broad range of evaluation metrics; it reports logit-difference and attention-score effects, including global versus local interventions.
Uses 15 templates and ABBA/BABA patterns in an aggregate dataset, but does not report circuit or performance results separately by prompt variant. It does not test prompts with more than two names.
